prompt: An admin created an account for a new employee in the Microsoft 365 admin center last week and configured nothing else. The employee can sign in but has no mailbox and cannot use Teams. What should the admin do?

options.text: Assign the employee a Microsoft 365 license in the admin center
Add the employee to the Members group of the company's SharePoint site
Add the employee to a distribution group in the Exchange admin center
Assign the employee the Exchange Administrator and Teams Administrator roles

explanation:
Services such as an Exchange Online mailbox and Teams are delivered through the service plans in a license. Assigning a license that includes them provisions the mailbox and turns on Teams.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the employee to the Members group of the company's SharePoint site: Site membership grants access to that site's content. It doesn't give the user a mailbox or Teams.
- Add the employee to a distribution group in the Exchange admin center: A distribution group only delivers email to its members' existing mailboxes. It can't create a mailbox for an unlicensed account.
- Assign the employee the Exchange Administrator and Teams Administrator roles: Admin roles let someone manage the Exchange and Teams services for others. They don't provision a mailbox or Teams access for the person who holds them; that comes from a license.

prompt: Every member of the Sales security group should receive Microsoft 365 E3 automatically when they join the group and lose it when they leave, with no per-user admin work. What should the admin do?

options.text: Assign the E3 license to each Sales user from the Active users page of the admin center
Assign the E3 license to the Sales group on the Licenses page of the admin center
Add the Sales group to the Members group of the Sales team's SharePoint site
Assign a Teams meeting policy to the Sales group with a group assignment ranking

explanation:
Group-based licensing assigns the license to the group. Members get it when they are added and lose it when they are removed, with no per-user work.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Assign the E3 license to each Sales user from the Active users page of the admin center: Direct assignment works, but the admin must license and unlicense every person by hand as people join and leave.
- Add the Sales group to the Members group of the Sales team's SharePoint site: That grants edit access to one site. It doesn't license anyone for Microsoft 365 services.
- Assign a Teams meeting policy to the Sales group with a group assignment ranking: Teams group policy assignment controls Teams behaviour. It doesn't assign Microsoft 365 licenses.

prompt: An admin assigned a Microsoft 365 license to the Employees group. Contractors are added only to a Contractors group, which is itself a member of Employees. Contractors report that they have no license. What should the admin do, with the least ongoing effort?

options.text: Make Employees a member of the Contractors group so the license flows into Contractors
Assign the license to each contractor individually from the Active users page
Assign the same license directly to the Contractors group as a second group assignment
Convert the Contractors group into a Microsoft 365 group and leave it nested in Employees

explanation:
Group-based licensing reaches only direct members of the licensed group. Licensing the Contractors group itself covers its members, and the license still follows membership automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Make Employees a member of the Contractors group so the license flows into Contractors: Reversing the nesting doesn't help: Employees holds the license, and nested membership still isn't used by group-based licensing.
- Assign the license to each contractor individually from the Active users page: This licenses the current contractors, but every new contractor must be licensed by hand, which is more ongoing effort than licensing the group.
- Convert the Contractors group into a Microsoft 365 group and leave it nested in Employees: The group type isn't the problem. Members of any nested group don't inherit the parent group's license assignment.

prompt: A security architect says every access request should be checked against the user's identity, device health, location and the data requested, even when the request comes from inside the corporate network. Which Zero Trust principle is this?

options.text: Use least privilege access
Assume breach
Defense in depth
Verify explicitly

explanation:
Verify explicitly means authenticating and authorizing every request using all available data points, with no trust granted for being on the internal network.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Use least privilege access: Least privilege limits how much access is granted (just-in-time, just-enough). It does not describe checking each request against identity, device and location signals.
- Assume breach: Assume breach is about limiting damage once an attacker is inside: segmentation, encryption and detection. The architect is describing how each request is checked.
- Defense in depth: Defense in depth is a general layering strategy, not one of the three Zero Trust principles Microsoft defines.

prompt: A 40-person company uses Microsoft 365 Business Basic, which includes only Microsoft Entra ID Free. It wants every user to register for and use multifactor authentication and wants legacy authentication blocked, without buying more licenses. What should the admin turn on?

options.text: Risk-based policies from Microsoft Entra ID Protection
A Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for each user
Security defaults for the Microsoft Entra tenant
Privileged Identity Management for admins

explanation:
Security defaults are free in every tenant. They require all users to register for MFA, prompt for it when needed, protect admin roles and block legacy authentication.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Risk-based policies from Microsoft Entra ID Protection: Risk-based policies need Microsoft Entra ID P2 and only act on risky users or sign-ins; they do not require MFA for everyone or block legacy authentication.
- A Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for each user: Conditional Access could enforce MFA, but creating policies needs Microsoft Entra ID P1, which the company does not have and does not want to buy.
- Privileged Identity Management for admins: PIM gives just-in-time access to admin roles and needs a P2 or ID Governance license. It does nothing for ordinary users' sign-ins.

prompt: All users have Microsoft 365 E3. The legal team must keep everything else in E3 but must not be able to use Microsoft Forms on any device or in the browser. Other departments keep Forms. What should the admin do?

options.text: Remove the Microsoft 365 E3 license from the legal team
Turn off Microsoft Forms in the legal team's E3 license assignment
Turn off the Microsoft Forms service on the Org settings page for the tenant
Block the Forms app for the legal team with a Teams app permission policy

explanation:
Each license is made of service plans, and individual apps and services can be switched off for a user's or group's assignment. That removes Forms for legal only while all other E3 services stay.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Remove the Microsoft 365 E3 license from the legal team: This removes Forms but also every other E3 service the legal team must keep, such as the mailbox and Teams.
- Turn off the Microsoft Forms service on the Org settings page for the tenant: Org settings apply to the whole organization. They can't remove Forms for one department while others keep it.
- Block the Forms app for the legal team with a Teams app permission policy: A Teams app permission policy only controls apps inside Teams. Legal could still open Forms in the browser.

prompt: A company segments access between departments, encrypts traffic end to end and uses analytics to spot unusual activity, planning on the basis that an attacker may already be inside. Which Zero Trust principle drives these measures?

options.text: Use least privilege access
Assume breach
Verify explicitly
Shared responsibility

explanation:
Assume breach means designing as if compromise has happened: minimize blast radius, segment access, encrypt end to end and use analytics to detect threats.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Use least privilege access: Least privilege limits each identity's rights. Segmentation, encryption and detection designed around an attacker already being inside belong to a different principle.
- Verify explicitly: Verify explicitly is about evaluating each request's signals at sign-in and access time, not about containing an intruder who is already present.
- Shared responsibility: Shared responsibility divides security duties between a cloud provider and its customer. It is not a Zero Trust principle.

prompt: A legal team wants contract drafts to stay protected so that only the legal department can open them, even after someone downloads a copy or emails it outside the company. Which Microsoft Purview feature should the admin use?

options.text: Sensitivity labels that apply encryption to drafts
A DLP policy that blocks sharing from the legal sites
Retention labels that mark the drafts as legal records
An Insider Risk Management policy for the legal team

explanation:
Encryption from a sensitivity label is stored with the file, so only the people the label authorizes can open it wherever the copy goes.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A DLP policy that blocks sharing from the legal sites: DLP can block or warn on sharing, but a copy that does get out isn't protected by it. The protection doesn't travel with the file.
- Retention labels that mark the drafts as legal records: A record label stops edits and deletion for a retention period. It doesn't control who can open a copy once it leaves the site.
- An Insider Risk Management policy for the legal team: Insider Risk Management detects risky activity patterns for investigation. It doesn't restrict who can open a document.

prompt: When users create a team for a confidential project, they pick a classification and the new team and its SharePoint site become private, with guest access blocked. No admin configures each site by hand. Which feature provides this?

options.text: Retention labels published to the SharePoint sites
DLP policies scoped to Teams chat and channel messages
Sensitivity labels configured for groups and sites
Retention policies scoped to Microsoft 365 groups

explanation:
Labels configured for groups and sites set container settings such as privacy and external user access when the label is chosen.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Retention labels published to the SharePoint sites: Retention labels apply retain/delete settings to individual items. They have no effect on team privacy or guests.
- DLP policies scoped to Teams chat and channel messages: DLP inspects messages and files for sensitive data. It doesn't set a team's privacy or who can be invited.
- Retention policies scoped to Microsoft 365 groups: Retention policies decide how long group content is kept or when it is deleted. They don't set privacy or guest access.

prompt: Thousands of existing files in SharePoint contain passport numbers. Nobody plans to open or edit them, but the compliance team wants them labeled Confidential. What should the admin configure?

options.text: A default sensitivity label in the label policy
Mandatory labeling in the label policy for SharePoint site members
Auto-labeling settings on the Confidential label for Office apps
An auto-labeling policy for SharePoint and OneDrive sites

explanation:
A service-side auto-labeling policy scans content at rest and labels matching files without any user opening them.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A default sensitivity label in the label policy: A default label is applied to new or unlabeled documents that users create or edit. Untouched files keep no label.
- Mandatory labeling in the label policy for SharePoint site members: Mandatory labeling forces users to pick a label when they save in an Office app. It does nothing for files no one is editing, whichever users the policy is published to.
- Auto-labeling settings on the Confidential label for Office apps: Client-side auto-labeling runs in the Office app while a user edits the file, so files nobody opens are never labeled.

prompt: A risk officer wants a percentage score that shows progress toward GDPR and ISO 27001 requirements across Microsoft 365, with recommended steps that can be assigned to staff and backed by uploaded evidence. Which tool should the admin open?

options.text: Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager
SharePoint data access governance reports
Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI reports
Microsoft Defender XDR Secure Score

explanation:
Compliance Manager scores progress against regulatory templates and lists improvement actions that can be assigned to owners, tested and supported with evidence files.

Why the other options are wrong:
- SharePoint data access governance reports: Data access governance reports show oversharing in SharePoint and OneDrive sites. They don't measure regulatory compliance.
- Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI reports: DSPM for AI reports on AI use and sensitive data in AI interactions. It doesn't track progress against regulatory controls.
- Microsoft Defender XDR Secure Score: Secure Score measures security configuration against Microsoft's recommendations. It isn't organised around regulations such as GDPR, and it has no evidence store for auditors.

prompt: A compliance admin wants Microsoft Purview to find credit card numbers in emails and documents by using a definition Microsoft already provides, without supplying any sample files. What should the admin use?

options.text: A pretrained trainable classifier
An exact data match classifier
A document fingerprint from a form
A sensitive information type

explanation:
Microsoft provides built-in sensitive information types, such as Credit Card Number, that match patterns, checksums and supporting keywords.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A pretrained trainable classifier: Trainable classifiers recognise kinds of documents, such as resumes, rather than a specific number format like a card number.
- An exact data match classifier: Exact data match needs you to upload your own table of values. The stem asks for something already provided.
- A document fingerprint from a form: Fingerprinting matches documents based on a form or template you supply, not individual card numbers.

prompt: A compliance admin opens the Improvement actions page in Compliance Manager for the first time. Under the shared responsibility model that Compliance Manager uses, which actions does this page list?

options.text: Actions that Microsoft completes for its own cloud services
Actions that DLP and insider risk alerts have asked admins to take
Actions that your organization is responsible for completing
Actions that both parties complete, with Microsoft testing them

explanation:
The Improvement actions page lists the actions your organization is responsible for; each can be assigned, implemented, tested and backed by evidence.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Actions that Microsoft completes for its own cloud services: Microsoft's share of the controls is handled and tested by Microsoft. Those actions aren't the ones on your Improvement actions page.
- Actions that DLP and insider risk alerts have asked admins to take: Alerts are handled in their own queues. Improvement actions are recommended configuration and process steps, not alert follow-ups.
- Actions that both parties complete, with Microsoft testing them: Compliance Manager doesn't split each action this way. Your actions are tested manually by you or automatically through signals from your tenant.

prompt: A company wants Microsoft Purview to find resumes and source code wherever they're stored. These files don't contain any consistent number pattern or keyword list. Which classification method fits best?

options.text: Custom sensitive information types with keyword lists
Document fingerprinting from a standard form
Built-in trainable classifiers for those categories
Exact data match with a table of known values

explanation:
Trainable classifiers recognise a kind of document by what it looks like overall, and Microsoft provides ready-made ones such as resumes and source code.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Custom sensitive information types with keyword lists: Keyword-based SITs need consistent terms or patterns, which the stem says these files don't have.
- Document fingerprinting from a standard form: Fingerprinting matches documents created from a template form. Resumes and code don't come from one template.
- Exact data match with a table of known values: Exact data match compares content with values from your own table, such as customer IDs. Resumes don't share such values.

prompt: Before rolling out Microsoft 365 Copilot, an admin needs to see which SharePoint sites, OneDrive accounts and mailboxes hold items already classified as containing credit card numbers, and drill down to each item. Which Microsoft Purview tool fits?

options.text: Data explorer in Information Protection
The DLP alerts page in the Purview portal
Activity explorer in Information Protection
Improvement actions in Compliance Manager

explanation:
Data explorer shows a current snapshot of items with sensitive information types, sensitivity labels, retention labels or trainable classifier matches, by location down to the item.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The DLP alerts page in the Purview portal: DLP alerts appear only when a policy rule matches an action. Items that nobody has shared or sent don't show up there.
- Activity explorer in Information Protection: Activity explorer lists actions taken on content, such as labels applied or DLP matches. It isn't an inventory of where classified items are stored.
- Improvement actions in Compliance Manager: Improvement actions are recommended configuration steps. They don't list the files and emails that contain sensitive data.

prompt: A company has Microsoft 365 E3 and no Copilot add-on licenses. In Copilot Chat on the web, outside Outlook, a user asks for a summary of what her manager emailed her about the budget this week, and the answer ignores her mailbox. What explains this?

options.text: The Allow web search in Copilot policy is off, which also stops mailbox lookups
Semantic indexing has not finished processing the users’ mailboxes yet
Restricted Content Discovery is hiding mailbox content from Copilot responses
Without a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, her mailbox isn’t used from there

explanation:
Outside Outlook, Copilot Chat included with Microsoft 365 answers from the web and from content the user supplies. It doesn’t reach into her mail, files or meetings through Microsoft Graph on its own.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The Allow web search in Copilot policy is off, which also stops mailbox lookups: That policy controls web grounding only. Turning it on or off has no effect on whether Copilot reads the mailbox.
- Semantic indexing has not finished processing the users’ mailboxes yet: Indexing delay could slow results for a licensed user, but an unlicensed Copilot Chat user has no Graph grounding to wait for.
- Restricted Content Discovery is hiding mailbox content from Copilot responses: Restricted Content Discovery applies to SharePoint sites, not Exchange mailboxes, and nothing in the scenario says it is configured.

prompt: Sales managers want Copilot to answer questions that draw automatically on their own emails, meetings and files, without uploading anything, and to work inside Word, Excel and PowerPoint with full access. The tenant currently uses only the Copilot Chat included with Microsoft 365. What should the admin do?

options.text: Assign Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses to the sales managers
Connect a pay-as-you-go billing policy for the sales managers
Turn on the Allow web search in Copilot policy for the sales managers
Pin Copilot Chat in Teams and Outlook for the sales managers

explanation:
The license adds automatic grounding in mail, meetings and files through Microsoft Graph and the full, priority in-app Copilot experience.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Connect a pay-as-you-go billing policy for the sales managers: Pay-as-you-go unlocks metered agents that use shared tenant content. It does not give each manager automatic grounding in their own mailbox and meetings across the apps.
- Turn on the Allow web search in Copilot policy for the sales managers: That policy adds or removes public web content. It does not give access to the managers’ own work data.
- Pin Copilot Chat in Teams and Outlook for the sales managers: Pinning makes Copilot Chat easier to find. It does not change what Copilot Chat is grounded in.

prompt: A company has bought Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses for 40 people in its finance department. Which admin center does the IT admin use to give those people the licenses?

options.text: Microsoft 365 Apps admin center
Microsoft 365 admin center
Microsoft Purview portal
Power Platform admin center

explanation:
Copilot licenses are managed under Billing > Licenses (or from a user’s Licenses and apps tab) in the Microsoft 365 admin center, for individual users or groups.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Microsoft 365 Apps admin center: This center manages Office app policies and update settings, such as cloud policies. It doesn’t assign licenses.
- Microsoft Purview portal: Purview handles data security and compliance, such as sensitivity labels and audit. License assignment isn’t done there.
- Power Platform admin center: This center governs environments and Copilot Studio agents. It doesn’t assign Microsoft 365 Copilot user licenses.

prompt: A marketing team without Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses wants an agent in Copilot Chat that follows written instructions and answers only from the company’s public website. How is this agent’s use paid for?

options.text: It needs each user to hold a Microsoft 365 Copilot license
It is billed per message to a pay-as-you-go billing policy
It needs a Copilot Studio capacity pack before anyone can use it
It is available at no additional cost in Copilot Chat

explanation:
Declarative agents grounded in instructions and public websites are included with Copilot Chat at no additional cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
- It needs each user to hold a Microsoft 365 Copilot license: Licensed users get work-data agents included, but web-only agents are already available to unlicensed Copilot Chat users.
- It is billed per message to a pay-as-you-go billing policy: Metered billing applies to agents that use shared tenant data such as SharePoint content, not to web-only agents.
- It needs a Copilot Studio capacity pack before anyone can use it: Prepaid capacity is one way to pay for metered agents. A web-only agent is not metered, so no capacity is needed.

prompt: Sales staff should get a Microsoft 365 Copilot license as soon as they are added to the Sales security group and lose it when they leave the group, without an admin acting on each change. What should the admin configure?

options.text: Add the Sales group to Copilot Frontier in Copilot settings
Assign the Copilot license to the Sales group itself
Assign the Copilot license to each Sales user as they join
Scope a pay-as-you-go billing policy to the Sales group

explanation:
Licensing the group means members receive the license when added and lose it when removed, with no per-user admin step.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the Sales group to Copilot Frontier in Copilot settings: Frontier controls early access to experimental features. It doesn’t assign or remove a Copilot license.
- Assign the Copilot license to each Sales user as they join: This works once, but someone must act on every join and leave, which the requirement rules out.
- Scope a pay-as-you-go billing policy to the Sales group: A billing policy pays for metered services such as agents for that group. It doesn’t give anyone a Copilot license.
